overview: Sigma 4.11's FakeHacker is a troll module that makes a chosen player look like a cheater on the local client. The target is a public static TARGET string (default 'NONE') set by the chat-prefixed FakeHackerTarget command, whose fire() handler only writes a local chat line via addChatMessage. Every update tick the module scans mc.theWorld.loadedEntityList for an entity whose name matches, and per enabled mode: KILLAURA aims the target's head and camera at the local player and swings the target's arm when it is within the RANGE setting (default 6.0); FLY snaps the target's posY to the local player's y plus 3 plus a randomized offset on a 100-tick counter; SPEED drifts the target's x and z by 0.1 toward its own yaw; SNEAK forces the sneak pose. The REACH and FLY branches that mutate C04/C06 packet fields are gated on EventPacket.isIncoming(), which is false for serverbound packets, so they never execute: the module's entire effect is local rendering and its wire footprint is zero.

sections.p: The module is one EventUpdate handler plus one EventPacket handler. The target comes from the public static TARGET field, which the FakeHackerTarget command sets by uppercasing its argument after validating args.length equals 1 and printing a local confirmation line through addChatMessage, so even the setup traffic is client-local. The settings are KILLAURA (default true), FLY, SPEED, SNEAK and REACH (all default false) plus RANGE, a Number setting with default 6.0, increment 0.1, and bounds 1 to 10. Each update tick the handler iterates the loaded entity list, matches entity names case-insensitively against TARGET, skips dead entities, and casts the match to EntityOtherPlayerMP without an instanceof guard.

KILLAURA computes the angles from the target toward the local player: getAnglesForThisEntityToHitYou takes the position difference with the player's eye height divided by 1.4, derives yaw from atan2 and pitch from the distance, and writes rotationYaw, rotationYawHead, rotationPitch and cameraPitch onto the target's entity, then calls swingItem() on it, so the victim's head tracks the player and its arm swings like an aura. FLY keeps a delay counter that resamples randomfly and randomfly2 (the local player's posY) every 100 ticks and sets the target's posY to randomfly2 plus 3 plus a randomized fraction, so the victim bobs roughly three blocks above the player. SPEED drifts the target's position by 0.1 per tick along the direction of its yaw minus 90 degrees, and SNEAK calls setSneaking(true). All four write only client-side state on a remote entity; the server's copy of the target never changes.

The EventPacket half is the interesting failure. REACH adds cos of (yaw minus 90) times 0.5 to the x and z of any C04PacketPlayerPosition or C06PacketPlayerPosLook, and FLY adds 1 to the y of any C04, but both branches are guarded by ep.isIncoming(). Sigma's NetworkManager fires EventPacket with the outgoing flag set to true in sendPacket for every packet the client sends, and with false in channelRead0 only for packets received from the server, so isIncoming(), which returns the negation of outgoing, is false for the serverbound C04/C06 family: the guards never pass and both branches are unreachable. The intended effect would have been a 0.5-block position shift toward the facing on the client's own movement stream (a crude reach assist) and a one-block y lift (a crude fly assist); as shipped, the module emits nothing.

files.label: FakeHacker.java
files.explanation: The six settings, the entity scan with the name match and dead-entity skip, the KILLAURA aim math with the eye-height divisor, the FLY position snapping, the SPEED drift, the SNEAK pose write, and the direction-inverted C04/C06 mutation branches that never fire. The TARGET static and the normalizeAngle helper are here too.

files.label: EventPacket.java (outgoing-flag semantics)
files.explanation: This event class carries the proof that the REACH and FLY packet branches are dead: fire(Packet, boolean outgoing) records the direction and isIncoming() returns the negation of outgoing. NetworkManager.sendPacket fires it with true and channelRead0 with false, so the serverbound C04/C06 instances the module checks can never satisfy isIncoming(). The module registers for exactly this event, which makes the inversion a property of the module's own guard rather than of the event system.

countering.label: Text (chat content and frequency scoring)
countering.explanation:
NCP's Text check scores every C01 chat message: an upper-case ratio beyond a third of the message length, letter-count and partition ratios for longer messages, per-word length and non-letter scores with the non-letter term squared, and a similarity comparison against the previous message within 8000ms, all folded into the chatFrequency and chatShortTermFrequency accumulators with the textFreqNormLevel and textFreqShortTermLevel floors.

The honest boundary: FakeHacker produces no serverbound traffic of its own, so no chat check can observe it. The theater it imitates surfaces in chat only if the user broadcasts accusations, and that broadcast stream is exactly what Text binds with its frequency floors and repetition penalty; the module itself stays under every threshold by emitting nothing. Text runs from ChatListener.onPlayerChat on the AsyncPlayerChatEvent at LOWEST priority, so it sees every message the module's user actually sends.

countering.label: Commands ('/' command rate)
countering.explanation:
NCP Commands weights every '/'-prefixed command at 1.0 into commandsWeights and compares the accumulated weight against commandsLevel plus the short-term window against commandsShortTermLevel, resetting the window when server lag exceeds 1.3. It runs from ChatListener.onPlayerCommandPreprocess, so only commands that reach the server count.

The FakeHackerTarget setup is handled by Sigma's chat-prefixed command system: its fire() writes a local message through addChatMessage and never queues a C01, so the setup produces no PlayerCommandPreprocess traffic either. Commands can therefore only bound the genuine '/'-commands the user types around the fake-hacker theater, and the module's zero-traffic behavior is invisible to it by construction, which is the honest statement of this entry: the check polices the surrounding command stream, not the module.

countering.label: Captcha (chat gate)
countering.explanation:
NCP Captcha is the enforcement end of the chat pipeline: shouldStartCaptcha auto-arms a challenge on chat violations, sendNewCaptcha generates a random captchaLength-character string, and checkCaptcha accepts only an exact equality between the incoming message and the stored captchaGenerated value, with wrong answers raising captchTries and captchaVL until the captchaTries threshold triggers the configured kick or ban actions.

For FakeHacker the gate is doubly unreachable: the module never sends chat, so it can never trip the frequency checks that arm the captcha, and the setup command is intercepted client-side before the wire. The captcha would only ever engage against the user's own spam, not against the module's behavior. The entry is therefore an honest boundary: it is the strongest chat-side enforcement available on the channel this module's category implies, and the module passes through it by emitting nothing, which is also why no server-side check can ever detect the module running.
